name: Mobile Developer Roadmap
tagline: From one native platform to offline-capable, push-enabled apps that pass review
summary: An ordered path for building production mobile applications. It starts with one platform learned properly — the language, its declarative UI toolkit and the lifecycle the operating system imposes — then adds the networking layer, because a mobile app is mostly a client for someone else's API on an unreliable connection. From there it moves through on-device storage and offline sync, the identity flows that differ from the web, live features such as push and sockets, and finally the release machinery: crash reporting, CI/CD and store review.

steps.label: Programming fundamentals
steps.note: Data structures, control flow and asynchrony come first because every mobile UI framework is built on callbacks, coroutines or async/await.

steps.label: Git & version control
steps.note: Branching and reviewing diffs are needed from the first team project, and mobile releases are cut from tags so the history has to be clean.

steps.label: Swift or Kotlin
steps.note: Pick iOS or Android and learn its language properly; splitting attention across both before either is comfortable produces two shallow skill sets.

steps.label: Declarative UI, navigation & app state
steps.note: SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose both re-render from state, so learning that model plus the platform's navigation stack and lifecycle callbacks unlocks most of the SDK.

steps.label: React Native or Flutter
steps.note: Worth learning after one native platform, so you can judge what a cross-platform runtime actually costs you and still drop to native code when it matters.

steps.label: HTTP
steps.note: Status codes, headers, caching and timeouts explain nearly every 'works on Wi-Fi, fails on cellular' bug report.

steps.label: REST APIs
steps.note: Most of an app's code consumes an API, so learn how resources, pagination and error bodies are conventionally shaped before designing screens around them.

steps.label: JSON & serialization
steps.note: Decoding into typed models is where a surprising share of crashes live: missing fields, nulls and schema changes shipped by the backend after your app is on devices.

steps.label: Networking on mobile
steps.note: Comes right after the basics because mobile networks are the differentiator: request coalescing, retries with backoff, timeouts, radio wake-up cost and battery all change how you call an API.

steps.label: Local storage with SQLite
steps.note: Once the app must show something before the network answers, you need a real local database rather than a pile of key-value preferences.

steps.label: Caching on device
steps.note: Images, API responses and rendered lists all need a cache with a size cap and an expiry policy, because device storage and memory are far smaller than a server's.

steps.label: Offline-first & sync
steps.note: The hardest mobile problem, and it only makes sense after storage and caching: queueing local writes, resolving conflicts on reconnect and keeping the UI honest about what has not synced yet.

steps.label: Authentication
steps.note: Login has to work across app restarts and long gaps, so sessions, refresh and biometric re-entry are designed differently from a web form.

steps.label: OAuth 2.0 in the system browser
steps.note: Third-party sign-in on mobile means an authorisation code flow with PKCE in the system browser, not a webview — this is where most first attempts get it wrong.

steps.label: JWT & secure token storage
steps.note: A shipped binary is on someone else's hardware, so tokens belong in the platform keychain or keystore and short expiry with silent refresh is the norm.

steps.label: Push notifications
steps.note: Placed after identity because a device token must be tied to a user, and after networking because delivery is best-effort — a push is a hint to sync, never the data itself.

steps.label: WebSocket
steps.note: Chat, presence and live scores need a persistent channel, and on mobile you also own reconnect on network change and teardown when the app is backgrounded.

steps.label: Crash reporting & observability
steps.note: You cannot attach a debugger to a user's phone, so symbolicated crash reports, breadcrumbs and adoption-per-version dashboards are the only view you get.

steps.label: CI/CD for mobile
steps.note: Signing certificates, provisioning profiles and store uploads are too error-prone to do by hand; automate the build and distribute to testers on every merge.

steps.label: App Store & Play review
steps.note: Last because it constrains everything before it: review guidelines, privacy disclosures, staged rollout and the fact that a bad release cannot be rolled back like a server deploy.
